## 1. Identification Strategy
Primary strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) using quasi-exogenous variation in the scheduled composition and visibility of co-workers to instrument contemporaneous peer productivity.

Rationale:
- The object of interest is the causal effect of peers’ productivity on a focal worker’s productivity. Simple OLS is plagued by simultaneity/reflection (co-workers respond to the same demand shocks and to each other in real time) and measurement error.
- We exploit two sources of plausibly exogenous variation:
  1) Bi-weekly schedules and staggered overlaps (set in advance and not tailored to short-run demand) determine which specific peers are on duty at each 10-minute interval.
  2) Register layout/orientation creates cross-sectional variation in which on-duty peers are mutually visible (and hence able to exert social pressure/monitoring).
- We instrument the realized average productivity of a focal worker’s visible co-workers with the predicted productivity of those same co-workers constructed from their pre-estimated, leave-out “ability” (long-run average productivity) interacted with on-duty and visibility at time t. Store-by-time fixed effects purge common demand shocks; comparisons are made across workers within the same store and 10-minute interval who face different visible peer sets.

This IV approach addresses the reflection problem and isolates contemporaneous social spillovers from common shocks. We then leverage visibility to separate social-pressure/monitoring from pure workload externalities.

Secondary design for mechanisms: Dynamic lead-lag/event-style analyses around changes in the visible peer set (e.g., arrivals/departures of high-ability visible peers) to distinguish contemporaneous social pressure from learning (persistence after the peer leaves).

## 2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):
  - peer_prod_vis_it: The leave-one-out average contemporaneous productivity (items per second) of worker i’s co-workers who are on duty and mutually visible to i in store s at 10-minute interval t.
  - For mechanism/placebo, also construct peer_prod_nonvis_it using on-duty but non-visible co-workers.

- Instrument(s):
  - z_vis_it: The average predicted productivity of i’s visible peers at time t, where predicted productivity for peer j is j’s leave-out long-run ability (e.g., mean items/sec computed excluding the current day or month), averaged over those j who are on duty and visible to i at t.
  - For the placebo/control arm, z_nonvis_it analogously for non-visible peers.

- Control group / counterfactual:
  - Within store × 10-minute cells, workers differ in who they can see. Workers whose visible peer sets are predicted to be lower-ability (z_vis low) serve as counterfactual to those whose visible peer sets are predicted to be higher-ability (z_vis high), netting out any store-time common shocks via high-dimensional fixed effects.
  - Non-visible peers form a natural placebo: estimated effects from non-visible peer productivity should be smaller if social monitoring drives the main effect.

- Treatment timing:
  - Continuous, contemporaneous at 10-minute intervals; robustness/event-style analyses around discrete changes in the visible peer set (e.g., when a high-ability visible peer starts/ends a shift).

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Relevance: Visible peers’ leave-out ability strongly predicts their realized contemporaneous productivity. Plausible given persistent individual differences in scanning speed; testable via first-stage F-statistics.

- Exclusion restriction: Conditional on store × 10-minute fixed effects and worker/register controls, the predicted ability of i’s visible peers affects i’s productivity only through those peers’ realized productivity/effort (and the associated social or workload mechanisms), not through omitted shocks directly affecting i.
  - Plausibility: Schedules are pre-set; visibility is determined by physical layout. Store-time fixed effects absorb demand and store-wide shocks. The mechanism of interest itself is “through peer productivity” (social pressure, monitoring, queue externalities), so the exclusion is coherent with the estimand.

- Independence/as-good-as-random assignment of the instrument within store × time:
  - Conditional on store × 10-minute fixed effects, differences in z_vis across workers arise from the interaction of a pre-set roster and fixed visibility network. Management does not purposefully pair high-ability teams in real time; within-cell composition differences are plausibly orthogonal to worker i’s idiosyncratic shocks.

- SUTVA/local spillovers structure: The relevant spillovers for i operate primarily through the defined peer sets (visible vs. non-visible). Broader store-wide shocks are absorbed by store-time fixed effects.

- Monotonicity: Increases in peers’ predicted ability do not decrease their own realized productivity on average (no “defiers” in the first stage).

## 4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
1) Endogenous register assignment/visibility exposure
   - Threat: Managers might assign faster workers to particular registers/lanes or positions with different visibility in response to anticipated demand patterns that also affect i.
   - Mitigation:
     - Include store × 10-minute fixed effects to purge all common time-varying store factors.
     - Add worker fixed effects and register fixed effects (or worker × register FE if feasible) to absorb persistent assignment patterns.
     - Show balance: visible-peer predicted ability is uncorrelated with pre-determined worker characteristics within store-time cells.
     - Robustness: Restrict to workers who remain on the same register within a shift; exclude first/last 20 minutes of shifts (when reassignments are more likely).

2) Reflection/common shocks
   - Threat: Realized peer productivity and focal productivity both respond to unobserved transient congestion or customer mix.
   - Mitigation:
     - Use IV based on peers’ leave-out ability, not their realized productivity.
     - Include fine fixed effects: store × 10-minute and rich diurnal patterns (day-of-week × hour FE).
     - Control for own workload composition (busy share, number of transactions) and team size.

3) Exclusion violation via unobserved co-determination of peer sets and focal productivity shocks
   - Threat: Peers’ schedules/preferences might correlate with focal workers’ unobservables (friend networks).
   - Mitigation:
     - Identification is within store-time; contemporaneous cross-worker comparisons rely on which peers are visible to whom given fixed layout, not on who is on shift overall.
     - Sensitivity: add pairwise worker-pair fixed effects for frequent dyads (where feasible) or limit to times when multiple possible visible peer configurations exist.
     - Placebo: estimate effect of non-visible peers; large effects there would suggest broader unaccounted channels.

## 5. R Code Outline
Note: This is an outline assuming CSV inputs with plausible schemas. Adjust variable names as needed.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)
library(readr)

# 1) Load data
tx <- fread("transactions.csv")       # cols: store_id, datetime, checker_id, register_id, items, seconds
ro <- fread("roster.csv")             # cols: store_id, datetime, checker_id, on_duty, register_id
vis <- fread("visible_pairs.csv")     # cols: store_id, register_id_i, register_id_j, visible_ij

# 2) Preprocess times and restrict sample
tx[, datetime := ymd_hms(datetime)]
ro[, datetime := ymd_hms(datetime)]
tx <- tx[hour(datetime) >= 7 & hour(datetime) < 20]
ro <- ro[hour(datetime) >= 7 & hour(datetime) < 20]
# 10-minute bins
tx[, time10 := floor_date(datetime, unit = "10 minutes")]
ro[, time10 := floor_date(datetime, unit = "10 minutes")]

# 3) Aggregate to checker x time10 productivity
tx_agg <- tx[, .(
  items = sum(items, na.rm = TRUE),
  secs  = sum(seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_trans = .N
), by = .(store_id, checker_id, register_id, time10)]
tx_agg[, prod := fifelse(secs > 0, items / secs, NA_real_)]
tx_agg[, busy_share := pmin(1, fifelse(secs > 0, secs / 600, 0))]

# 4) On-duty roster by register at time10
ro_duty <- ro[on_duty == 1, .(store_id, time10, checker_id, register_id)]
# Merge productivity onto roster (fill zeros for no transactions)
dt <- merge(ro_duty, tx_agg[, .(store_id, checker_id, time10, prod, busy_share, n_trans)],
            by = c("store_id","checker_id","time10"), all.x = TRUE)
dt[is.na(prod), prod := 0]         # when on-duty but no transactions, set prod=0; alternatively drop or flag
dt[is.na(busy_share), busy_share := 0]
dt[is.na(n_trans), n_trans := 0]

# 5) Compute worker ability (leave-out long-run mean)
# Option A: leave-one-day-out mean
dt[, date := as.Date(time10)]
ability_all <- dt[, .(ability = mean(prod, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(checker_id)]
dt <- merge(dt, ability_all, by = "checker_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 6) Build visible and non-visible peer sets within store x time10
# Map current register occupancy to visibility graph
setkey(dt, store_id, time10, register_id)
setkey(vis, store_id, register_id_i)

# Create pairs: i (focal) at register r_i, j (peer) at register r_j
pairs <- merge(
  dt[, .(store_id, time10, checker_id_i = checker_id, register_id_i = register_id,
         prod_junk = prod, ability_i = ability)],  # prod_junk not used; ability_i for checks
  vis, by = c("store_id","register_id_i"), allow.cartesian = TRUE
)
# Attach who is at register_j at time t
setkey(pairs, store_id, time10, register_id_j)
setkey(dt,    store_id, time10, register_id)
pairs <- merge(
  pairs,
  dt[, .(store_id, time10, register_id = register_id,
         checker_id_j = checker_id, prod_j = prod, ability_j = ability)],
  by.x = c("store_id","time10","register_id_j"),
  by.y = c("store_id","time10","register_id"),
  all.x = TRUE, allow.cartesian = TRUE
)
# Drop self-pairs and missing peers
pairs <- pairs[checker_id_i != checker_id_j & !is.na(checker_id_j)]

# Aggregate to focal i x time10: visible and non-visible averages
peer_agg <- pairs[, .(
  peer_prod_vis    = mean(prod_j[visible_ij == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
  peer_prod_nonvis = mean(prod_j[visible_ij == 0], na.rm = TRUE),
  z_vis            = mean(ability_j[visible_ij == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
  z_nonvis         = mean(ability_j[visible_ij == 0], na.rm = TRUE),
  n_vis_peers      = sum(visible_ij == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_nonvis_peers   = sum(visible_ij == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = .(store_id, time10, checker_id_i)]

setnames(peer_agg, "checker_id_i", "checker_id")

# 7) Merge peer aggregates back to focal data
dt2 <- merge(dt, peer_agg, by = c("store_id","time10","checker_id"), all.x = TRUE)
# Replace NaNs when no peers in category
for (v in c("peer_prod_vis","peer_prod_nonvis","z_vis","z_nonvis")) {
  dt2[is.nan(get(v)) | is.infinite(get(v)), (v) := NA_real_]
}
dt2[is.na(n_vis_peers), n_vis_peers := 0]
dt2[is.na(n_nonvis_peers), n_nonvis_peers := 0]

# 8) Fixed effects and clustering variables
dt2[, store_time_fe := interaction(store_id, time10, drop = TRUE)]
dt2[, worker_fe := checker_id]
dt2[, store_day := interaction(store_id, as.Date(time10), drop = TRUE)]

# 9) Main 2SLS: effect of visible peers (instrumented) on focal productivity
# Keep observations with at least one visible peer (for main effect)
main_sample <- dt2[n_vis_peers > 0]

# Controls: busy_share, team size; FE: store x time, worker
est_main <- feols(
  prod ~ busy_share + n_vis_peers | store_time_fe + worker_fe |
    (peer_prod_vis ~ z_vis),
  data = main_sample,
  cluster = ~ store_day # cluster at store-day
)
summary(est_main)

# 10) Robustness: include non-visible peer productivity with its instrument (placebo)
rb_sample <- dt2[n_vis_peers > 0 & n_nonvis_peers > 0]
est_rb <- feols(
  prod ~ busy_share + n_vis_peers + n_nonvis_peers | store_time_fe + worker_fe |
    (peer_prod_vis + peer_prod_nonvis ~ z_vis + z_nonvis),
  data = rb_sample,
  cluster = ~ store_day
)
summary(est_rb)

# 11) Additional robustness: drop windows around shift changes (peer set instability)
# Identify changes in visible peer set for each worker
setorder(dt2, checker_id, time10)
dt2[, vis_hash := paste0(store_id, ":", time10, ":", n_vis_peers)]
dt2[, vis_change := (shift(vis_hash, type = "lag") != vis_hash), by = checker_id]
# Drop +/- 20 minutes (2 bins) around changes
dt2[, drop_window := vis_change | shift(vis_change, 1L, type = "lead") | shift(vis_change, 2L, type = "lead") |
                    shift(vis_change, 1L, type = "lag")  | shift(vis_change, 2L, type = "lag"), by = checker_id]
clean_sample <- dt2[n_vis_peers > 0 & !drop_window]
est_clean <- feols(
  prod ~ busy_share + n_vis_peers | store_time_fe + worker_fe |
    (peer_prod_vis ~ z_vis),
  data = clean_sample,
  cluster = ~ store_day
)
summary(est_clean)

# 12) First-stage diagnostics
fs <- fitfixef(est_main, stage = 1)
summary(fs)
```

Notes:
- If zero-output intervals are conceptually “idle time,” you may prefer to condition on busy intervals or include busy_share as a control as shown.
- For ability_j, you can implement stricter leave-one-period-out (e.g., leave-one-month-out) and verify robustness.

## 6. Expected Results
- Direction: Positive contemporaneous spillovers from visible peers’ productivity to the focal worker’s productivity, consistent with social pressure/mutual monitoring and contagious effort. Smaller or no effect from non-visible peers after controlling for store-time shocks (placebo).
- Magnitude: A 10% increase in visible peers’ productivity predicted by the instrument could raise focal productivity by about 1–3% contemporaneously (elasticity ~0.1–0.3). Effects should be strongest when:
  - Mutual visibility is high,
  - Teams are larger/queues thick (peer comparison salient),
  - Among less-experienced workers (if knowledge transmission contributes).
- Dynamics: Limited persistence after the high-ability visible peer leaves (consistent with social pressure). Any persistence would suggest knowledge transmission.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
- C1: Instrument relevance (strong first stage within store×time) = 1
- C2: Exclusion (peer ability affects focal output only via peers’ realized productivity) = 1
- C3: Independence/as-good-as-random conditional on store×time and worker FEs = 1
- C4: Monotonicity (higher peer ability weakly increases peers’ own productivity) = 1
- C5: SUTVA/limited interference outside defined peer sets (within-cell) = 0

Overall, the design directly addresses simultaneity via IV, nets out common shocks with fine FEs, and uses visibility to separate social monitoring from pure workload externalities. Robustness checks (placebo with non-visible peers, dropping shift-change windows, alternative ability definitions) further strengthen credibility.
